title: Book 2, Chapter 7 — Second Year of the War—The Plague of Athens—Position and Policy of Pericles—Fall of Potidæa
paragraphs: Such was the funeral that took place during this winter, with which the first year of the war came to an end. In the early days of summer the Lacedaemonians and their allies, with two-thirds of their forces as before, invaded Attica under the command of Archidamus, son of Zeuxidamus, king of Lacedaemon, and sat down and laid waste the country. Not many days after their arrival in Attica, the plague first began to show itself among the Athenians. It was said it had broken out in many places previously around Lemnos and elsewhere, but a pestilence of such extent and mortality was nowhere remembered. The doctors at first were of no help, since they did not know the right way to treat it; in fact they died themselves the most thickly, since they visited the sick most often. Nor did any human art succeed any better. Supplications in the temples, divinations, and the like proved equally futile, until in the end the overwhelming nature of the disaster put a stop to them altogether.

It first began, it is said, in the parts of Ethiopia above Egypt, and from there came down into Egypt and Libya and into most of the King’s country. Falling suddenly on Athens, it first attacked the population in Piraeus — which gave rise to the saying that the Peloponnesians had poisoned the reservoirs, since there were as yet no wells there — and afterwards appeared in the upper city, when the deaths became much more frequent. All speculation about its origin and its causes — if causes can be found great enough to produce such a disturbance — I leave to other writers, professional or otherwise. For myself, I will simply set down its nature and explain the symptoms by which it may perhaps be recognized by the student, if it should ever break out again. This I can do all the better since I had the disease myself and watched its course in others.

That year, then, is admitted to have been otherwise unprecedentedly free from sickness; and what few cases did occur all ended in this. As a rule, however, there was no obvious cause; people in good health were suddenly attacked by violent fevers in the head, with redness and inflammation in the eyes; the inward parts, like the throat or tongue, became bloody and gave off an unnatural and fetid breath. These symptoms were followed by sneezing and hoarseness, after which the pain soon reached the chest and produced a hard cough. When it settled in the stomach, it upset it, and discharges of bile of every kind named by physicians followed, accompanied by very great distress. In most cases an ineffectual retching also followed, producing violent spasms — which in some cases ceased soon after, in others much later. Externally the body was not very hot to the touch, nor pale in colour, but reddish, livid, and breaking out in small pustules and ulcers. Internally, however, it burned so that the patient could not bear even the lightest clothing or linen on him, but had to be stark naked. What they would have liked best was to throw themselves into cold water; some of the neglected sick actually did so, plunging into the rain-tanks in their agonies of unquenchable thirst, though it made no difference whether they drank little or much. Besides this, the wretched feeling of being unable to rest or sleep never stopped tormenting them. The body, meanwhile, did not waste away as long as the disease was at its height, but held out remarkably against its ravages; so that when most of them succumbed on the seventh or eighth day to the internal inflammation, they still had some strength left in them. But if they passed this stage and the disease descended further into the bowels, producing a violent ulceration there with severe diarrhoea, this brought on a weakness that was generally fatal. The disorder first settled in the head, ran its course from there through the whole body, and even where it did not prove fatal, it left its mark on the extremities; for it settled in the privy parts, the fingers, and the toes, and many escaped with the loss of these — some too with the loss of their eyes. Others again, on first recovering, were seized with a complete loss of memory and did not know either themselves or their friends.

But while the nature of the disease was such as to baffle all description, and its attacks almost too grievous for human nature to endure, it was in the following respect that its difference from all ordinary disorders was most clearly shown. All the birds and beasts that prey on human bodies either kept away from them — though many lay unburied — or died after tasting them. As proof of this, it was noticed that birds of this kind actually disappeared; they were not around the bodies, or indeed to be seen at all. Of course the effects I have mentioned could best be studied in a domestic animal like the dog.

These, then, if we set aside the many peculiar variations from case to case, were the general features of the disease. Meanwhile the city was free of all the usual disorders, or, if any case did occur, it ended in this one. Some died in neglect, others in the midst of every attention. No remedy was found that could be relied on as a specific; what helped one patient harmed another. Strong and weak constitutions proved equally incapable of resisting; all alike were swept away, even those nursed with the utmost care. By far the most terrible feature of the malady was the despair that came over anyone who felt himself sickening: the moment they fell into it, their power of resistance was gone, and they became a much easier prey to the disease. On top of this there was the appalling spectacle of men dying like sheep, having caught the infection while nursing each other. This caused the greatest mortality. On the one hand, if they were afraid to visit one another, they perished from neglect; many houses were emptied of their inmates for want of a nurse. On the other, if they ventured to do so, death was the consequence. This was especially the case with those who made any pretensions to goodness: honour made them unsparing of themselves in their attendance on their friends, when even the members of the family were at last worn out by the moans of the dying and overwhelmed by the force of the disaster. Yet it was with those who had recovered from the disease that the sick and the dying found most compassion. They knew what it was from experience, and now had no fear for themselves, since the same man was never attacked twice — never at least fatally. Such people not only received the congratulations of others, but in the elation of the moment half entertained the vain hope that they were now safe from any disease whatsoever.

An aggravation of the existing calamity was the influx from the country into the city, and this was felt especially by the new arrivals. Since there were no houses to receive them, they had to be lodged at the hot time of the year in stifling cabins, where the mortality raged unchecked. The bodies of dying men lay one on top of another, and half-dead creatures reeled about the streets and gathered round all the fountains in their longing for water. The sacred places too in which they had quartered themselves were full of corpses of those who had died there, just as they were; for as the disaster passed all bounds, men, not knowing what was to become of them, became utterly careless of everything, sacred or profane. All the burial rites previously in use were entirely upset, and they buried the bodies as best they could. Many, lacking the proper means because so many of their friends had already died, resorted to the most shameless burials. Sometimes, getting in ahead of those who had built a pyre, they threw their own dead body on the stranger’s pyre and lit it; sometimes they tossed the corpse they were carrying on top of another that was already burning, and went off.

Nor was this the only form of lawless excess to which the plague gave rise. Men now coolly ventured on what they had previously done in a corner, and not just as they pleased — seeing the rapid changes of fortune as people in prosperity suddenly died and those who before had nothing succeeded to their property. So they resolved to spend quickly and enjoy themselves, regarding lives and riches alike as things of a day. Perseverance in what was called honour was popular with no one; it was so uncertain whether they would be spared to attain the goal. Present enjoyment, and whatever contributed to it, was settled to be honourable and useful. Fear of the gods or law of men there was none to restrain them. As for the gods, they judged it made no difference whether they worshipped them or not, since they saw all alike perishing; as for the laws, no one expected to live to be brought to trial for his offences. Each man felt that a far harsher sentence had already been passed on them all and was hanging over their heads, and that, before this fell, it was only reasonable to enjoy life a little.

Such was the nature of the calamity, and heavily did it weigh on the Athenians: death raging within the city and devastation outside it. Among other things they remembered in their distress was, very naturally, the following verse, which the old men said had long ago been uttered:
A Dorian war shall come and with it death.

A dispute arose as to whether the word in the verse had not been “dearth” rather than “death”; but at the present moment it was of course decided in favour of “death,” since people made their memory fit their sufferings. I imagine, though, that if another Dorian war should ever come on us, and a dearth should happen to accompany it, the verse will probably be read accordingly. The oracle that had been given to the Lacedaemonians was now also remembered by those who knew of it. When the god was asked whether they should go to war, he answered that if they put their full strength into it, victory would be theirs, and that he himself would be with them. With this oracle events were thought to tally. The plague broke out as soon as the Peloponnesians invaded Attica; it never entered the Peloponnese, at least not to any noticeable extent; and it did its worst in Athens, and after Athens, in the most populous of the other towns. Such was the history of the plague.

After ravaging the plain, the Peloponnesians advanced into the Paralian region as far as Laurium, where the Athenian silver mines are. They first laid waste the side facing the Peloponnese, then the side facing Euboea and Andros. But Pericles, who was still general, held the same view as in the previous invasion, and would not let the Athenians march out against them.

While the Peloponnesians were still in the plain, however, and had not yet entered the Paralian land, he had prepared a force of a hundred ships against the Peloponnese, and once everything was ready he put out to sea. He took on board four thousand Athenian heavy infantry and three hundred cavalry in horse transports — converted then for the first time from old galleys; fifty Chian and Lesbian ships also joined the expedition. When this Athenian force put out to sea, they left the Peloponnesians in Attica in the Paralian region. Reaching Epidaurus in the Peloponnese, they ravaged most of the territory and even had hopes of taking the town by assault, though in this they did not succeed. Putting out from Epidaurus, they laid waste the territory of Troezen, Halieis, and Hermione, all towns on the coast of the Peloponnese, and from there sailed to Prasiai, a maritime town in Laconia, ravaged part of its territory, and took and sacked the place itself. After this they returned home, but found the Peloponnesians gone and no longer in Attica.

All the time the Peloponnesians were in Attica and the Athenians on the expedition in their ships, men kept dying of the plague both in the fleet and in Athens. It was even claimed that the departure of the Peloponnesians was hastened by fear of the disease, since they heard from deserters that it was in the city, and could see the burials going on. Yet on this invasion they stayed longer than on any other, and ravaged the whole country, since they were about forty days in Attica.

The same summer Hagnon, son of Nicias, and Cleopompus, son of Clinias, the colleagues of Pericles, took the force he had recently used and went off on an expedition against the Chalcidians around Thrace and Potidæa, which was still under siege. As soon as they arrived, they brought up their engines against Potidæa and tried every means of taking it, but did not succeed in capturing the city or in doing anything else worthy of their preparations. The plague attacked them here too, and committed such havoc as to cripple them completely; even the previously healthy soldiers from the earlier expedition caught the infection from Hagnon’s troops, while Phormio and the sixteen hundred men under his command escaped only by being no longer in the area of the Chalcidians. The end of it was that Hagnon returned with his ships to Athens, having lost one thousand and fifty out of four thousand heavy infantry in about forty days; though the soldiers stationed there before stayed in the country and carried on the siege of Potidæa.

After the second Peloponnesian invasion a change came over the Athenians’ spirit. Their land had now been twice laid waste, and war and pestilence pressed heavily on them at once. They began to find fault with Pericles as the author of the war and the cause of all their misfortunes, and grew eager to come to terms with Lacedaemon, even sending ambassadors there, who, however, did not succeed in their mission. Their despair was now complete, and all of it was vented on Pericles. When he saw them exasperated at the present turn of events and acting exactly as he had foreseen, he called an assembly — being, remember, still general — with the double aim of restoring confidence and of leading them out of these angry feelings into a calmer and more hopeful frame of mind. So he came forward and spoke as follows:

“I was not unprepared for the indignation directed at me — I know its causes — and I have called this assembly to remind you of certain points and to protest against your being unreasonably angry with me, or cowed by your sufferings. In my view, the greatness of the state is more for the advantage of private citizens than any individual prosperity coupled with public humiliation. A man may personally be ever so well off, and yet if his country is ruined he must be ruined with it; whereas a flourishing commonwealth always offers chances of safety to unfortunate individuals. Since, then, a state can support the misfortunes of private citizens but they cannot support hers, surely it is the duty of every man to come forward in her defence, and not, as you are doing now, to be so overwhelmed with your private afflictions that you give up all thought of the common safety, and blame me for advising war and yourselves for voting it. And yet, if you are angry with me, it is with one who, I believe, is second to no man either in knowing the right policy or in the ability to expound it, and who is moreover not only a patriot but an honest one. A man who has the knowledge but not the gift of expression might as well have no idea on the matter at all; if he had both gifts but no love for his country, he would be only a cold advocate for her interests; and if his patriotism were not proof against bribery, everything would go for a price. So if you thought I was even moderately distinguished for these qualities when you took my advice and went to war, there is certainly no reason now why I should be charged with having done wrong.

“For those, of course, who have a free choice in the matter and whose fortunes are not at stake, war is the greatest of follies. But if the only choice is between submission with loss of independence, and danger with the hope of preserving that independence, then it is the man who will not accept the risk who deserves blame, not the one who will. I am the same man and do not change; it is you who change. In fact, you took my advice while you were unhurt, and have waited for misfortune to make you regret it; and the apparent error of my policy lies in the weakness of your resolve, since the suffering it brings is being felt by every one of you, while its advantage is still remote and obscure to all. A great and sudden reverse having befallen you, your minds are too depressed to keep to your resolutions. Before what is sudden, unexpected, and least to be calculated on, the spirit quails; and, putting everything else aside, the plague has certainly been an emergency of this kind. Born, however, as you are, citizens of a great state, and brought up with habits to match your birth, you should be ready to face the greatest disasters and still keep the lustre of your name unimpaired. The judgement of mankind is as relentless toward the weakness that falls short of a known reputation as it is jealous of the arrogance that aims higher than its due. Stop grieving over your private afflictions, then, and address yourselves instead to the safety of the commonwealth.

“If you shrink from the efforts the war makes necessary, and fear that even so they may not have a happy outcome, you know the reasons by which I have often shown you that your fears are groundless. If those are not enough, I will now disclose an advantage arising from the greatness of your dominion, which I do not think has yet occurred to you, and which I never mentioned in my earlier speeches. It has so bold a sound that I would scarcely venture it now, were it not for the unnatural depression I see around me. You perhaps think that your empire extends only over your allies; I will tell you the truth. The visible field of action has two parts, land and sea. In the whole of one of these you are completely supreme — not only as far as you currently use it, but to whatever further extent you may think fit. In short, your naval resources are such that your ships may go where they please, with neither the King nor any other nation on earth able to stop them. So, although you may think it a great hardship to lose the use of your land and houses, you must see that this power is something far different. Instead of fretting over them, you should really regard them as the gardens and other accessories that adorn a great fortune, and as, by comparison, of little importance. You should also know that liberty preserved by your efforts will easily recover for us what we have lost, while once the knee is bowed, even what you have will pass from you. Your fathers received these possessions not from others but from themselves, and did not let slip what their labour had won, but delivered them safely to you. In this respect at least you must prove yourselves their equals, remembering that to lose what one has got is more disgraceful than to be balked in getting it. You must confront your enemies not merely with spirit but with disdain. Confidence indeed a blissful ignorance can give, even to a coward’s breast; but disdain is the privilege of those who, like us, have been assured by reflection of their superiority over their adversary. And where the chances are even, knowledge fortifies courage by the contempt that follows from it; its trust is placed not in hope, the prop of the desperate, but in a judgement based on existing resources, whose anticipations can be more relied upon.

“Again, your country has a right to your services in sustaining the glories of her position. These are a common source of pride to you all, and you cannot decline the burdens of empire and still expect to share its honours. Remember too that what you are fighting against is not merely slavery instead of independence, but also loss of empire and the danger from the resentments incurred in exercising it. Besides, retreat is no longer possible, even if any of you, alarmed by the moment, has fallen in love with the apparent honesty of an unambitious course. For what you hold is, to put it plainly, a tyranny: to take it perhaps was wrong, but to let it go is unsafe. And men of these retiring views, making converts of others, would quickly ruin a state; the result would be the same even if they could live independently by themselves, since the retiring and unambitious are never secure without vigorous protectors at their side. In short, such qualities are useless to an imperial city, though they may help a dependency to an unmolested servitude.

“But you must not be misled by citizens of this kind, or angry with me — who, if I voted for war, did only as you yourselves did — even though the enemy has invaded your country and done what you could be sure he would do if you refused to comply with his demands; and even though, on top of what we counted on, the plague has come on us — the only point at which our calculation has been at fault. I know this has done much to make me more unpopular than I would otherwise have been — quite undeservedly, unless you are also prepared to give me the credit for any success that chance may bring. Besides, the hand of heaven must be borne with resignation, the hand of the enemy with fortitude. This was the old way at Athens, and let it not now be otherwise. Remember too that if your country has the greatest name in all the world, it is because she has never bent before disaster; because she has spent more lives and effort in war than any other city, and has won for herself a power greater than any yet known, the memory of which will pass down to the latest posterity. Even if now, in obedience to the general law of decay, we should ever be forced to yield, it will still be remembered that we ruled over more Hellenes than any other Hellenic state, that we sustained the greatest wars against their united and separate powers, and inhabited a city unrivalled in resources or size. These glories may incur the censure of the slow and unambitious, but they will rouse emulation in the breasts of the energetic, and in those who must remain without them an envious regret. Hatred and unpopularity in the moment have always been the lot of those who have aspired to rule others; but where odium must be incurred, true wisdom incurs it for the highest objects. Hatred too is short-lived; but what makes the splendour of the present and the glory of the future endures forever unforgotten. Make your decision, then, for glory hereafter and honour now, and gain both by instant and zealous effort. Do not send heralds to Lacedaemon, and show no sign of being weighed down by your present sufferings; for those whose minds are least sensitive to disaster, and whose hands are quickest to meet it, are the greatest men and the greatest communities.”

Such were the arguments by which Pericles tried to cure the Athenians of their anger against him and to turn their thoughts from their immediate afflictions. As a community he succeeded in convincing them; they not only gave up all idea of sending to Lacedaemon but applied themselves with renewed energy to the war. Still, as private individuals, they could not help smarting under their sufferings — the common people having lost the little they had, while the higher orders had lost fine properties with costly establishments and buildings in the country, and, worst of all, had war instead of peace. The public feeling against him in fact did not subside until they had fined him. Not long after, however, in the way of the multitude, they elected him general again and put all their affairs in his hands, having now grown less sensitive to their private and domestic afflictions and seeing that he was the best man for the public needs. As long as he was at the head of the state during the peace, he pursued a moderate and conservative policy; and in his time its greatness was at its height. When the war broke out, here too he seems to have rightly gauged the power of his country. He outlived its outbreak by two years and six months, and after his death the correctness of his foresight became more apparent. He told them to wait quietly, to attend to their navy, to attempt no new conquests, and to expose the city to no risks during the war; and on these conditions he promised them a favourable outcome. They did the very opposite. Allowing private ambitions and private interests, in matters apparently quite unconnected with the war, to lead them into projects unjust both to themselves and to their allies — projects whose success would only bring honour and advantage to private persons, and whose failure brought certain disaster on the country in the war. The reasons are not far to seek. Pericles, by his rank, ability, and known integrity, was able to exercise an independent control over the multitude — to lead them, in short, instead of being led by them. Since he never sought power by improper means, he was never compelled to flatter them, but, on the contrary, was held in such high regard that he could afford to anger them by contradiction. Whenever he saw them unseasonably and insolently elated, he could with a word reduce them to alarm; if, on the other hand, they fell into a panic, he could at once restore them to confidence. In short, what was nominally a democracy became in his hands government by the first citizen. With his successors it was different. More on a level with one another, and each grasping at supremacy, they ended by handing even the conduct of state affairs over to the whims of the multitude. This, as might have been expected in a great and sovereign state, produced a host of blunders, among them the Sicilian expedition — though this failed not so much through a miscalculation of the power of those it was sent against, as through a fault in the senders, who failed to take the best measures afterwards to support those who had gone out, choosing instead to occupy themselves with private intrigues for the leadership of the people. By this they not only paralysed operations in the field but also first introduced civil discord at home. Yet after losing most of their fleet, along with other forces, in Sicily, and with faction already dominant in the city, they could still for three years hold out against their original adversaries, joined now not only by the Sicilians but by their own allies, nearly all in revolt, and at last by the King’s son, Cyrus, who supplied the funds for the Peloponnesian navy. Nor did they finally succumb until they fell victim to their own internal disorders. So abundantly more than enough were the resources from which the genius of Pericles foresaw an easy victory in the war over the unaided forces of the Peloponnesians.

During the same summer the Lacedaemonians and their allies made an expedition with a hundred ships against Zacynthus, an island off the coast of Elis, peopled by a colony of Achaeans from the Peloponnese and in alliance with Athens. There were a thousand Lacedaemonian heavy infantry on board, and Cnemus, a Spartan, as admiral. They made a landing from their ships and ravaged most of the country; but as the inhabitants would not submit, they sailed home.

At the end of the same summer Aristeus the Corinthian, Aneristus, Nicolaus, and Stratodemus — envoys from Lacedaemon — Timagoras, a Tegean, and a private individual named Pollis from Argos, on their way to Asia to persuade the King to supply funds and join the war, came to Sitalces, son of Teres, in Thrace. Their idea was to induce him, if possible, to abandon the Athenian alliance and march on Potidæa, then under siege by an Athenian force, and also to be conveyed by his help across the Hellespont to Pharnabazus, who would send them up country to the King. But there happened to be with Sitalces some Athenian ambassadors — Learchus, son of Callimachus, and Ameiniades, son of Philemon — who persuaded Sitalces’ son Sadocus, the new Athenian citizen, to put the men into their hands and so prevent their crossing over to the King and helping to harm the country he had chosen. Sadocus accordingly had them seized as they were travelling through Thrace to the ship in which they were to cross the Hellespont. The seizure was carried out by a party he had sent on with Learchus and Ameiniades, with orders to deliver the men to the Athenian ambassadors, who brought them to Athens. On their arrival, the Athenians, afraid that Aristeus, who had notably been the prime mover in earlier affairs at Potidæa and in their Thracian possessions, might survive to do them still more harm if he escaped, killed them all the same day, without granting them a trial or hearing the defence they wished to offer, and threw their bodies into a pit. They thought themselves justified in using in retaliation the same kind of warfare that the Lacedaemonians had begun, when they had killed and thrown into pits all the Athenian and allied traders they caught on board the merchantmen round the Peloponnese. Indeed, at the start of the war, the Lacedaemonians butchered as enemies all whom they took at sea, whether allies of Athens or neutrals.

About the same time, towards the close of the summer, the Ambraciot forces, with a number of barbarians they had raised, marched against Amphilochian Argos and the rest of that country. The origin of their enmity against the Argives was this. This Argos and the rest of Amphilochia were colonized by Amphilochus, son of Amphiaraus. Dissatisfied with the state of affairs at home on his return after the Trojan War, he built this city in the Ambracian Gulf and named it Argos after his own country. This was the largest town in Amphilochia, and its inhabitants the most powerful. Generations later, under the pressure of misfortune, they called in the Ambraciots, their neighbours on the Amphilochian border, to join their colony. It was through this union with the Ambraciots that they learned their present Hellenic speech; the rest of the Amphilochians are barbarians. After a time the Ambraciots expelled the Argives and held the city themselves. At this the Amphilochians threw in their lot with the Acarnanians, and together they called in the Athenians, who sent them Phormio as general with thirty ships; on whose arrival they took Argos by storm and made slaves of the Ambraciots. The Amphilochians and Acarnanians then inhabited the town in common. After this began the alliance between Athenians and Acarnanians. The enmity of the Ambraciots toward the Argives thus dates from the enslavement of their citizens; and afterwards, during the war, they collected this force from among themselves, the Chaonians, and other neighbouring barbarians. Arriving before Argos, they became masters of the country; but failing in their attacks on the town, they returned home and dispersed among their various peoples.

Such were the events of the summer. The following winter the Athenians sent twenty ships round the Peloponnese, under the command of Phormio, who stationed himself at Naupactus and kept watch on anyone sailing in or out of Corinth and the Crissaean Gulf. Six others went to Caria and Lycia under Melesander to collect tribute in those parts, and also to prevent the Peloponnesian privateers from setting up a base in those waters and harassing the passage of merchantmen from Phaselis, Phoenicia, and the adjoining mainland. Melesander, however, going up country into Lycia with a force of Athenians from the ships and the allies, was defeated and killed in battle, with the loss of a number of his troops.

The same winter the Potidæans at last found themselves no longer able to hold out against their besiegers. The Peloponnesian invasions of Attica had not had the desired effect of making the Athenians raise the siege. Provisions were exhausted, and distress for food in Potidæa had gone so far that, among many other horrors, instances had even occurred of people eating one another. In this extremity they at last made proposals to capitulate to the Athenian generals in command against them — Xenophon, son of Euripides, Hestiodorus, son of Aristocleides, and Phanomachus, son of Callimachus. The generals accepted their proposals, seeing the suffering of the army in such an exposed position; besides, the state had already spent two thousand talents on the siege. The terms of capitulation were as follows: free passage out for themselves, their children, wives, and auxiliaries, with one garment apiece, two for the women, and a fixed sum of money for their journey. Under this treaty they went out to Chalcidice and other places, as their means allowed. The Athenians, however, blamed the generals for granting terms without instructions from home, holding that the place would have had to surrender at discretion. They afterwards sent their own settlers to Potidæa and colonized it. Such were the events of the winter; and so ended the second year of this war of which Thucydides was the historian.
